concept.sub_category: Range and spread of a numeric list

examples.problem_statement: List K consists of the numbers −10, −5, 0, 5, and 10. Which of the following lists of numbers have the same range as the numbers in list K ? Indicate all such lists. (A) −15, −1, 0, 1, 15  (B) −7, −4, −2, 1, 13  (C) 0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 10  (D) 2, 3, 5, 15, 19, 22  (E) 4, 5, 6, 24

solution.result: definition to apply to every list
solution.description: Recall the definition the whole question turns on: a list's range is the difference between its greatest and its least number.
Apply that definition to list K, whose greatest number is 10 and least number is -10, to get the target range every answer choice must match.

solution.result: only the two end numbers of each choice matter
solution.description: Notice that in every choice the numbers are already listed from least to greatest, so you only need to read the first and last number of a list rather than scan all of it.
Take the end numbers of Choice A, greatest 15 and least -15, subtract, and compare the result with 20; it does not match.
Do the same subtraction for Choice B, greatest 13 and least -7, and find a range equal to the target 20.
Subtract Choice C's least number 0 from its greatest number 10; the range is half the target, so this list is rejected.
Subtract Choice D's least number 2 from its greatest number 22 and find the range equals the target 20.
Subtract Choice E's least number 4 from its greatest number 24 and find the range again equals the target 20.

solution.result: the three lists whose range is 20
solution.description: Collect every choice whose computed range came out to 20 and select all of them, since the question asks you to indicate all such lists.

examples.answer: Choice B: − 7, − 4, − 2, 1, 13 AND Choice D: 2, 3, 5, 15, 19, 22 AND Choice E: 4, 5, 6, 24

key_reminders: Range is greatest minus least, so it depends only on the two extreme values, never on the count of numbers in between.
Subtracting a negative least value adds its magnitude: 13 - (-7) = 13 + 7.
When a list is already written in increasing order, its extremes are the first and last entries.
common_mistakes: Reading list K's range as 10 by using the largest value alone instead of subtracting the least value -10.
Sign-slipping on Choices A and B, where the least number is negative, and computing 15 - 15 = 0 or 13 - 7 = 6.
Stopping after finding one matching list, when this multi-select question has three correct choices.

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. Through its state associations, the American Medical Association controlled who could become a physician and dominated ______ professions like nursing and occupational therapy. (A) commensurate (B) proportionate (C) kindred (D) affiliated (E) imperative (F) voluntary

solution.operation: blank \to \text{describes nursing and occupational therapy relative to physicians}
solution.result: the blank needs a word for the relation between those professions and physicians
solution.description: Read what the blank is doing in the sentence: it must describe professions such as nursing and occupational therapy as they relate to physicians.

solution.result: a word signalling a close relationship is required
solution.description: Use the sentence's own examples as the clue: these professions are also in the health-care field, so the blank calls for a word suggesting that close relationship.

solution.result: a pair that both fit and are alike in meaning
solution.description: Test the choices against that requirement and find that kindred and affiliated both suggest the close relationship and produce two completed sentences similar in meaning.
Rule out commensurate and proportionate because they suggest a comparative measurement between the professions, something the rest of the sentence gives no support for.

solution.result: both rejected, and neither has a partner
solution.description: Rule out imperative and voluntary because neither would typically describe a profession, and neither has a close-in-meaning partner among the remaining choices to pair with.

examples.answer: Choice C: kindred; AND Choice D: affiliated

key_reminders: The two correct choices must both fit the sentence and produce completed sentences alike in meaning.
A choice with no meaning-partner among the other options cannot be part of the answer pair.
Only a relationship the sentence itself supports counts; do not import an idea the text never states.
common_mistakes: Pairing commensurate with proportionate because they are synonyms, ignoring that the sentence never sets up a comparison of measure.
Choosing a single best word and stopping, when this format requires exactly two.

examples.problem_statement: Ethanol, a fuel derived from corn, can be used alone to power vehicles or along with gasoline to reduce the amount of gasoline consumed. Compared with conventional gasoline, pure ethanol produces significantly less pollution per gallon used. In order to combat pollution, many individuals advocate the increased usage of ethanol as a fuel source for vehicles in conjunction with or in place of gasoline. In evaluating the recommendation to increase the use of ethanol, it would be most important to research which of the following? (A) Whether the majority of existing vehicles are capable of using ethanol for fuel, either alone or in conjunction with gasoline (B) Whether the process of growing corn to produce ethanol results in significant amounts of pollution (C) Whether completely replacing gasoline with ethanol results in less pollution than using ethanol in conjunction with gasoline (D) Whether ethanol is more expensive to produce than conventional gasoline (E) Whether there are some vehicles in which using ethanol fuel would not result in a significant reduction in pollution compared to conventional gasoline

solution.description: Identify the question type from the stem: it asks what would be most important to research in evaluating a recommendation, which marks it as an Evaluate question.

solution.operation: \text{eth OR eth}+\text{gas can power veh};\ \text{PURE eth pollution} < \text{gas}
solution.result: two premises, the second only about pure ethanol
solution.description: Deconstruct the premises and map them: ethanol alone or with gasoline can power vehicles, and pure ethanol pollutes less per gallon than gasoline, noting that the second fact covers only pure ethanol.

solution.result: the conclusion, stated in terms of pollution
solution.description: Mark the conclusion: to combat pollution we should increase ethanol use, alone or with gasoline. It is specifically about reducing pollution.

solution.operation: \text{right answer: strengthens if answered one way, weakens if answered the other}
solution.result: the goal for testing each choice
solution.description: State the goal for an Evaluate question: the correct choice must be able to both strengthen and weaken the argument, showing the ethanol plan might cut pollution or might not, and it must actually mention pollution.

Test choice A: if most vehicles can use ethanol the plan proceeds, but if they cannot, switching as many as possible would still reduce pollution. It says switching might be difficult, not that it would fail to reduce pollution.

Test choice B: if growing corn produces a lot of pollution the switch would not actually cut pollution, while if ethanol can be produced cleanly the switch cuts pollution a lot. It swings the argument either way, which is what an Evaluate answer must do.
Test choice C: it splits apart the two options the conclusion combines, and knowing which of them pollutes less still says nothing about whether either beats pure gasoline.
Test choice D: production cost may be a drawback of ethanol generally, but the conclusion is about pollution, not cost, so cost cannot evaluate this argument.
Test choice E: it speaks only of some vehicles, and without knowing how many, it tells you neither that the overall switch would work nor that it would not.

key_reminders: An Evaluate answer must be able to cut both ways: answered one way it strengthens the plan, answered the other it weakens it.
The right answer has to bear on the conclusion's own terms, which here is pollution, not cost or feasibility.
Work from wrong to right, eliminating four choices rather than hunting for the one that sounds best.
common_mistakes: Picking (D) because cost feels like a real objection to ethanol, though the conclusion is about pollution only.
Picking (A) by treating a practical obstacle to adoption as evidence that pollution would not fall.
Picking (E) without noticing that 'some vehicles' gives no quantity, so it cannot swing the argument either way.

concept.technique_name: two-blank text completion by charge matching

examples.problem_statement: Select one entry for each blank from the corresponding column of choices, filling all blanks in the way that best completes the text. At their best, (i) ______ book reviews are written in defense of value and in the tacit hope that the author, having had his or her (ii) ______ pointed out, might secretly agree that the book could be improved. Blank (i): (A) abstruse (B) adverse (C) hortatory. Blank (ii): (D) strengths (E) transgressions (F) assumptions.

solution.operation: \text{clue: author might agree the book could be improved}
solution.description: Use the second half of the sentence as the clue for Blank (ii): whatever is pointed out makes the author concede the book could be improved, so it must be something negative whose presence calls for improvement.
Scan the Blank (ii) column against that requirement; transgressions is the only choice negative in meaning, so it fills the second blank.

solution.result: Blank (i) must also be negative in meaning
solution.description: Carry that result back to the first blank: reviews that point out an author's transgressions are negative in nature, so Blank (i) needs a negative word too.
Check the Blank (i) column for a negative word; adverse is the only choice that meets the condition, so it fills the first blank.

examples.answer: Choice B: adverse; AND Choice E: transgressions

key_reminders: Fill the blank whose clue is most explicit first, then use that filled word as the clue for the remaining blank.
Matching the charge of the word, positive or negative, is often enough to isolate the single valid choice in a column.
Each blank draws only from its own column of choices.
common_mistakes: Starting at Blank (i), where all three words are unfamiliar in tone, instead of at Blank (ii), where the clue is explicit.
Choosing 'strengths' for Blank (ii) by reading 'in defense of value' as praise, which contradicts the book needing improvement.
Confusing 'adverse' with 'averse' and rejecting it as describing a person rather than the reviews.
